meta.titre: Pragmatism and the Scientific Method: Peirce's four ways of settling belief and the practical test of truth
meta.sous_theme: Peirce, James and Dewey: belief, inquiry and truth

sections.contenu_markdown: A farmer near Bamenda hears that a new fertiliser doubles the harvest. One neighbour believes it because the village elders say so, another believes it because he has always believed in new products, and a third tries it on a small plot and compares the result with an untreated plot. These are three ways of holding the same belief. American pragmatists asked which way deserves our trust and what truth finally means. The GCE examines their answers in short questions on definitions and in essays that ask whether usefulness is a test of truth.

items: A belief is something a person holds to be true; a hypothesis is a proposed explanation that can be tested.
One traditional view says that a statement is true when it matches reality.
A scientific experiment compares a prediction with observation.

sections.titre: Pragmatism: the maxim, the fixation of belief and the practical test of truth
sections.contenu_markdown:
### What pragmatism is
**Pragmatism** is an American movement of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. It was founded by Charles Sanders Peirce and developed by William James and John Dewey. Its core idea is that beliefs, concepts and theories should be judged by their practical consequences: what difference they make to experience and action. The doctrine that a theory is true when it works in practice is the **pragmatic theory of truth**, associated above all with James.

### Peirce: meaning, doubt and belief
- **Pragmatic maxim**: the meaning of a concept lies in its conceivable practical effects. If two ideas would have no different practical effects, there is no real difference between them.
- **Doubt and belief**: doubt is an uneasy, irritating state that pushes us to inquire. Belief is the calm state in which inquiry ends and which guides action as a habit. Belief therefore lies between doubt and action.

### Peirce's four methods of fixing belief
| Method | How belief is fixed | Weakness |
|---|---|---|
| Tenacity | Hold on to what one already believes and avoid contrary evidence | Contact with people who think differently disturbs it |
| Authority | A state or institution imposes the beliefs | It cannot control every opinion, and people see societies with other beliefs |
| A priori | Adopt what seems agreeable to reason | It depends on taste and fashion, with no check from reality |
| Science | Beliefs are determined by real things whose character is independent of what anyone thinks | Self-correcting; the only method that can tell a right way of reasoning from a wrong one |

Peirce defends the method of **science**. Its assumption is that there are real things independent of our opinions, so that people who investigate honestly will in the end reach the same conclusion. For Peirce, truth is the opinion on which all investigators would finally agree.

### James and Dewey
James held that a true idea is one that can be verified and that leads us satisfactorily through experience; truth is made in the course of experience. Dewey called his view **instrumentalism**: ideas are tools for solving problems, and inquiry is a process that moves from a problematic situation to a settled one. Peirce disliked the loose way James used his maxim and later called his own position pragmaticism.

### Criticisms
Critics ask: works for whom, and for how long? A comforting falsehood may be useful for a time, so usefulness and truth seem different. Pragmatists reply that truth means what survives testing in the long run, not private convenience.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When one term or doctrine is asked for
variantes.contenu_markdown: Memorise the pairs: pragmatism is the doctrine linking truth to practical success; the method of science is the one that rests on realities independent of opinion; belief lies between doubt and action; the founder is Peirce; instrumentalism belongs to Dewey.

variantes.nom: Essay on the pragmatic theory of truth
variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to assess or discuss the claim that truth is what works
variantes.contenu_markdown: Plan: define the theory; give supporting reasons (it links ideas to experience and gives a clear test); give objections (useful falsehoods, vagueness of "works", conflict with correspondence); give the reply (long-run, verified success); judge.

sections.enonce_markdown: Using Peirce's account, explain why a community that settles belief by authority may eventually have to move toward the scientific method.

etapes.justification: The answer depends on knowing exactly what authority is and what science is.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Tenacity, authority, a priori and science; authority means beliefs imposed by an institution.

etapes.justification: Fairness requires you to show why the method was attractive.
etapes.resultat_markdown: It gives a community stable and shared beliefs, and it removes doubt for many people.

etapes.justification: Peirce's objection is that the social impulse and contact with other societies reveal alternative beliefs.
etapes.resultat_markdown: If a rumour imposed by an elder council says that a certain herb cures a disease, patients who keep falling sick will doubt it; doubt returns and inquiry begins again.

etapes.action: Show why science answers the problem.
etapes.justification: Science rests on realities independent of opinion, so it can settle doubt in a lasting way.
etapes.resultat_markdown: A fair test, for example comparing recovery rates, would give results that do not depend on who holds office.

etapes.justification: A conclusion shows that the question has been answered, not just described.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Authority may calm doubt for a time, but because doubt returns when beliefs conflict with experience, a community will tend to need the self-correcting method of science.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Model answer, key points: (1) Peirce says doubt irritates and belief settles. (2) Authority fixes belief by imposition and gives stability. (3) Contact with other opinions and with experience revives doubt. (4) Science relies on realities independent of opinion and corrects itself through testing. (5) So a community that begins with authority will eventually be pushed toward science.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing that the method of science is the method of what most people believe.
items.pourquoi_faux: Peirce's method of science depends on realities independent of anyone's opinion.
items.correction_markdown: What decides the matter is evidence from real things, not majority opinion.

items.erreur_markdown: Calling the method of authority "a priori" because it appeals to reason.
items.pourquoi_faux: Authority rests on imposed belief; the a priori method rests on what seems agreeable to reason.
items.correction_markdown: Keep the four names and their means distinct: tenacity (holding on), authority (imposed), a priori (agreeable to reason), science (independent reality).

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that pragmatism teaches that anything that benefits me is true.
items.pourquoi_faux: For pragmatists, truth must be verified in experience, and James meant success tested over time, not private convenience.
items.correction_markdown: Pragmatism links truth to verified practical consequences; it does not make personal advantage the test.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that for Peirce doubt is a pleasant state and belief an uneasy one.
items.pourquoi_faux: It is the other way round: doubt irritates and belief settles.
items.correction_markdown: Doubt stimulates inquiry; belief ends it and guides action.

items.enonce_markdown: Name Peirce's four methods of fixing belief and say which one he defends.
items.solution_markdown:
- Tenacity, authority, a priori and science.
- Peirce defends the method of science.
**Award a mark for each method and one for the defended method.**

items.enonce_markdown: A town council orders that everyone must accept an official account of the town's origins and punishes those who question it. Which of Peirce's methods does this resemble, and what weakness would he point out?
items.solution_markdown:
- It resembles the method of **authority**.
- Peirce's weakness: the authority cannot control every opinion, and people who meet other societies with other beliefs begin to doubt.
**Award a mark for naming the method and one for the weakness.**

items.enonce_markdown: Assess the view that a belief is true only if it is useful.
items.solution_markdown:
- Support: pragmatists tie meaning and truth to experience; a belief that never guides successful action is of little worth.
- Objection: a useful falsehood, such as a comforting but untrue belief about an illness, shows that usefulness and truth can differ; "useful to whom?" is also unclear.
- Reply: Pragmatists reply that truth means verification by experience over the long run, tested by many people; Peirce's own version defines truth by the agreement of all honest investigators.
**Judgement: usefulness is a good sign of truth but cannot simply be identified with it.**

items_markdown: Pragmatism judges beliefs and theories by their practical consequences; the pragmatic theory of truth links truth to what works.
Peirce's maxim: the meaning of a concept lies in its conceivable practical effects.
Doubt irritates and starts inquiry; belief settles inquiry and guides action, so belief lies between doubt and action.
Peirce's four methods are tenacity, authority, a priori and science; he defends science because it rests on realities independent of opinion.
James tied truth to verification in experience; Dewey called ideas instruments for solving problems.
The standard objection is that useful falsehoods exist; pragmatists reply that truth is tested in the long run.
